title: Student work and study study
transcript:
[00:00:05] INT: Thanks again for coming in today, Callum MacLeod. Just to confirm for the recording, you have read the participant information sheet and signed the consent form, and you are happy for me to record this?
[00:00:18] P: Aye, that is totally fine. Happy to go ahead.
[00:00:22] INT: Brilliant. So, just to start off with a bit of background, could you tell me a little bit about yourself, what you are studying, and how you came to be at university here in Glasgow?
[00:00:34] P: Sure. Well, I am 19 years old, in my second year at the University of West Clyde, studying History and Politics. I am the first person in my family to go to uni, actually. My mum, Fiona MacLeod, worked in a care home for twenty years, and my dad was a joiner before he retired early. Growing up in Govan, uni always felt like something other people did, you know? Nobody on my street really went. When I got my offer from UWC, Fiona was over the moon, honestly, she framed the letter and put it on the mantelpiece.
[00:01:12] INT: That sounds like a really proud moment for her. Did you stay at home in Govan for first year, or did you move out?
[00:01:20] P: I stayed at home for first year just to save a bit of cash, commuting across the river every morning. Then this year I moved into a shared flat with two mates from my course. We are at 42 Byres Terrace, Partick, Glasgow. It is a decent enough wee flat, right near the subway, which makes getting to lectures and getting to work a lot easier. Rent is £485 a month before bills, which is actually not bad for Partick these days, though it still eats up most of my student loan.
[00:01:55] INT: And how are you finding the financial side of things overall? Is that what prompted you to take on part-time work?
[00:02:03] P: Oh, definitely. My student funding works out to about £620 a month once you average it out over the academic year. After rent, gas, electricity, and the Wi-Fi, I am left with barely anything for food or bus fares. So I had to get a job pretty much straight away when term started. I started at Clydeview Retail Group on 14 September 2024. Most people just call it Clydeview, or CRG if you are looking at the payslips. I work in the stockroom and warehouse at their big superstore out towards the west end.
[00:02:41] INT: What kind of hours are you doing at Clydeview, and what is the pay like?
[00:02:47] P: I am contracted for sixteen hours a week, usually two eight-hour shifts, one on a Friday night and one on a Sunday. Though they are always texting me asking if I can pick up overtime. The pay is £11.44 an hour, which is just the minimum wage for my age bracket, well, actually they pay everyone the adult rate there regardless of age, which is fair enough. It keeps my head above water. My goal is to try and save £1,200 by the summer so I do not have to panic about rent over July and August when the student funding stops.
[00:03:26] INT: That is a big target to aim for alongside a full-time degree. Tell me a bit about what the actual work involves and what the people are like there.
[00:03:35] P: It is pretty physical, to be honest. Unloading pallets, breaking down cages, restocking the heavy stuff like drinks and pet food before the store opens. My line manager is Mrs Patricia Boyle. She is quite strict about timekeeping, very by-the-book, you know? If you are two minutes late clocking in, Boyle is straight on your case. To be fair to Patricia, she does try to work around my exam timetable if I give her enough notice, so I cannot complain too much. Most of my shifts are alongside a guy called Liam Donnelly. Liam is a couple of years older than me, not a student, just works there full-time. He is a good laugh, makes the night shifts bearable.
[00:04:22] INT: Are there many other students working in the warehouse with you?
[00:04:26] P: A few on the checkouts, maybe two or three in the back, but most of them only do daytime weekends. I ended up doing the late shifts because the bus back to Partick is quiet and I get the daytime free for the library. Actually, because I have been there a bit longer than the other part-timers now, I am the only student trained to operate the industrial cardboard baler on the night shift. It sounds dead boring, I know, but it means they rely on me quite heavily on Friday nights. Sometimes I feel guilty saying no to extra shifts because I know Liam gets stuck doing all the bailing himself if I am not in.
[00:05:08] INT: That sounds like quite a lot of responsibility for a part-time role. How does that balance out with your studies at UWC?
[00:05:17] P: It is a constant juggling act, Callum trying to be in two places at once, as my mum says. When things are quiet in October, it is fine. I go to my lectures, do my reading, work my shifts, no bother. The problem is when deadlines cluster together. Like back on 3 November 2024, I had two two-thousand-word essays due on the same Monday, and CRG had a massive pre-Christmas delivery coming in that weekend. I ended up working twenty-four hours over Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, and then pulled an all-nighter to finish my Politics essay.
[00:05:56] INT: How did that affect your coursework, or did you speak to anyone at the university about it?
[00:06:02] P: I scraped a pass on the Politics one, which I was gutted about because I usually get high sixties. After that, I went to see my academic adviser, Dr Alistair Kerr. I was a bit nervous about telling him I was working so many hours because you always hear lecturers say you should treat uni like a full-time job. But Dr Kerr was actually brilliant about it. He said loads of students at the University of West Clyde are in the same boat, especially first-generation students who do not have parents sending them money every month. He helped me map out my deadlines for the next semester and showed me how to apply for a short extension if things get out of hand again.
[00:06:48] INT: That is really good to hear that Dr Kerr was supportive. Have you noticed the workload taking a toll on your health at all?
[00:06:57] P: Yeah, a bit, if I am being completely honest. I have had asthma since I was a wee boy, and the warehouse at Clydeview is really dusty, especially when you are breaking down cardboard all night. I have been going through my blue inhaler a lot quicker than I used to. And then on the mental health side, I was diagnosed with generalised anxiety back in sixth year of high school. I take sertraline every morning, which mostly keeps it steady, but when I am running on four hours of sleep after a night shift and worrying about essays, my chest gets tight and I start panicking about failing out.
[00:07:40] INT: That sounds really tough to manage alongside everything else. Does your manager know about your asthma or the anxiety?
[00:07:48] P: She knows about the asthma because I had to put it on the health and safety form when I started, and I keep my inhaler in my locker. I have not told Patricia about the anxiety, though. I just do not want them thinking I cannot handle the shifts or cutting my hours. I need the money too much.
[00:08:08] INT: That makes complete sense. Have you had any administrative headaches trying to juggle the university and the job, like with tax or student status?
[00:08:18] P: Oh, do not even get me started. Last month HR at Clydeview put me on an emergency tax code by mistake, so I lost nearly a hundred quid off my payslip. I had to spend two hours on the phone and send them a letter from the uni proving I was a full-time student, with my student ID number UWC-2024-88412 and my employee reference number CRG-77319 all matched up. It got sorted eventually, and they refunded me on the next pay run, but it was a massive stress when rent was due.
[00:08:53] INT: When you are not working or studying, do you get any downtime at all? How do you switch off?
[00:09:00] P: Not as much as I would like, to be honest. I do not really go out clubbing much because it costs too much and I am usually knackered. My main way of unwinding is a bit of a weird one, actually. I am really into restoring vintage 1950s mechanical typewriters. My grandad gave me an old Olympia before he passed away, and I just got hooked on taking them apart, cleaning the keys, and getting them working again. I pick them up cheap at car boot sales or charity shops around Glasgow. It is completely offline, no screens, just tinkering with springs and ribbons for an hour before bed. It really calms my head down.
[00:09:44] INT: That is a fantastic hobby, very tactile and completely different from staring at a laptop all day. Looking ahead to the rest of the academic year, what are your main priorities?
[00:09:56] P: Just getting through the January exam block in one piece, really. My first exam is on 20 January 2025, so I have already put my holiday request in at CRG for the week before. Once I get through second year, I am hoping to apply for a paid internship over the summer, maybe something related to my degree, though if not, I will just pick up extra hours at Clydeview.
[00:10:22] INT: Well, I really hope the exams go well for you. Just before we wrap up, we send out a £25 shopping voucher as a thank you for taking part in the study, and we also send a short summary of the findings once the project finishes. What is the best email address and phone number to reach you on?
[00:10:41] P: Brilliant, thank you. My email is callum.macleod19@example.org, and my mobile is 07700 900412.
[00:10:52] INT: Got it. Thanks so much for your time today, Callum, I really appreciate you being so open about your experiences.
[00:10:59] P: No problem at all, happy to help.
